AlphaGo played South Korean professional Go player [Lee Sedol](/wiki/Lee_Sedol "Lee Sedol"), ranked 9-dan, one of the best players at Go,[[16]](#cite_note-CNN0128-16) with five games taking place at the [Four Seasons Hotel](/wiki/Four_Seasons_Hotel "Four Seasons Hotel") in [Seoul](/wiki/Seoul "Seoul"), South Korea on 9, 10, 12, 13, and 15 March 2016,[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-25) which were video-streamed live.[[26]](#cite_note-26) Out of five games, AlphaGo won four games and Lee won the fourth game which made him recorded as the only human player who beat AlphaGo in all of its 74 official games.[[27]](#cite_note-koreatimes_beatable-27) AlphaGo ran on Google's cloud computing with its servers located in the United States.[[28]](#cite_note-JoongAng_Ilbo-28) The match used [Chinese rules](/wiki/Rules_of_go#Chinese_rules "Rules of go") with a 7.5-point [komi](/wiki/Komidashi "Komidashi"), and each side had two hours of thinking time plus three 60-second [byoyomi](/wiki/Byoyomi "Byoyomi") periods.[[29]](#cite_note-Korea_Baduk_Association-29) The version of AlphaGo playing against Lee used a similar amount of computing power as was used in the Fan Hui match.[[30]](#cite_note-30) *[The Economist](/wiki/The_Economist "The Economist")* reported that it used 1,920 [CPUs](/wiki/Central_processing_unit "Central processing unit") and 280 [GPUs](/wiki/Graphics_processing_unit "Graphics processing unit").[[31]](#cite_note-31) At the time of play, Lee Sedol had the second-highest number of Go international championship victories in the world after South Korean player [Lee Chang-ho](/wiki/Lee_Chang-ho "Lee Chang-ho") who kept the world championship title for 16 years.[[32]](#cite_note-32) Since there is no single official method of [ranking in international Go](/wiki/Go_ranks_and_ratings#Rating_systems "Go ranks and ratings"), the rankings may vary among the sources.
